summary: OAuth works through an external client app (or legacy connected app) configured in Setup. No Salesforce approval is needed for OAuth itself, but a big change just landed: creating new connected apps is restricted as of Spring '26, and Salesforce pushes external client apps instead.

approval.typical_timeline: Creating the external client app and running OAuth: same day. AppExchange listing is a separate security review (details not verified in this pass).
approval.notes: As of Spring '26 you cannot create new connected apps without contacting Salesforce Support; use external client apps.

steps.title: Create an external client app in Setup
steps.detail: Setup -> Apps -> External Client Apps. Legacy path (New Connected App) is restricted as of Spring '26 and requires contacting Salesforce Support.

steps.title: Enable OAuth settings
steps.detail: Configure callback URL and OAuth scopes for the API integration.

steps.title: Pick the right OAuth flow
steps.detail: Salesforce supports several OAuth 2.0 flows; each is a three-step pattern: request access, receive tokens, resource server validates them.

steps.title: Test against a sandbox or developer edition org
steps.detail: Use a free Developer Edition org to exercise the flow before pointing at a customer org.

nuances: The connected-app to external-client-app transition is recent; older tutorials and Stack Overflow answers still describe the deprecated path.
Org admins control whether users can self-authorize the app or installs need admin pre-approval.
AppExchange distribution involves Salesforce's security review, which is a much bigger lift than OAuth setup.
agent_can_do: Tell you whether current docs mean external client app or connected app for your org version
Generate the OAuth flow for your chosen grant type
Keep your plan aligned with the Spring '26 change
human_must_do: Create the external client app with your Salesforce admin
Decide install policies for customer orgs
Drive AppExchange security review if you list
